abstract: This paper examines how labor-market institutions shape environmental policy design when regulators choose the timing of command-and-control regulation. We develop a theoretical model of a unionized oligopoly in which a welfare-maximizing regulator imposes a uniform emissions-intensity standard either before wage-setting or after wages have been set. The key mechanism is that environmental policy and wage bargaining interact strategically when unions attach value to environmental quality. Under ex-ante regulation, environmental standards influence subsequent wage-setting, whereas under ex-post regulation wage-setting influences the regulator's policy choice. As a result, regulatory timing determines not only environmental stringency, but also wages, output, and welfare. We show, first, that union environmental awareness affects regulatory incentives differently across the two-timing regimes. Under ex-ante regulation, greater union environmental concern raises the negotiated wage at a given emissions intensity but also strengthens the wage moderation induced by cleaner production. These opposing effects on output incentives can generate a non-monotonic relationship between union greenness and optimal regulatory stringency. Under ex-post regulation, greater union environmental awareness raises wages, contracts output and induces the regulator to relax the environmental standard. Second, the comparison between ex-ante and ex-post regulation is parameter-dependent: the regimes can differ in environmental stringency, wages, output, and emissions, with the relevant rankings changing at well-defined thresholds. Third, the welfare effects of regulatory timing are conditional rather than uniform. Ex-ante regulation can be welfare-superior when its beneficial effect on output outweighs the welfare loss from departing from the optimal standard for the given output. The welfare value of regulatory commitment therefore depends on how union environmental preferences interact with wage bargaining and production incentives. The central timing mechanism remains relevant under decentralized wage bargaining, environmentally concerned firms, and scale-dependent compliance costs.
title: Environmental policy design under unionized wage-setting: Regulatory timing and green preferences

abstract: Buffer zones are intended to facilitate the management of anthropogenic pressures surrounding protected areas; however, empirical evidence regarding characteristics of these pressures before and after buffer zone implementation remains limited. This study investigates impervious land cover surfaces (used as a proxy for land-use changes associated with urban development) and cropland coverage to assess how land cover change patterns have evolved within the buffer zones of fifteen South African National Parks from 2000 to 2022, using the GLC_FCS30D dataset. We found that policy-designated buffer zones shape land cover around PAs only to a limited extent. Following designation, development-related trajectories generally remained stable or slowed, while agricultural trajectories showed no significant change. The study compares trends in two buffer zone types, i.e., Priority Natural Areas (PNAs) and Viewshed Protection Areas (VPAs), before and after implementation to describe directional changes over time. Trends before and after implementation were quantified using segmented regression analysis. Most PNAs demonstrated stable impervious surface trajectories with no significant change in growth rate post-implementation, whereas several VPAs exhibited deceleration in impervious surface growth rate. Conversely, cropland trajectories were more variable across buffer types, exhibiting both accelerations and decelerations in growth rates, indicating that agricultural expansion remains a more dynamic and influential land-use driver within buffer zones. Shifts in cropland, therefore, remain a key concern and likely require greater policy focus and stronger coordination across conservation, planning, and agricultural sectors.
title: Do policy-designated buffer zones shape land cover trajectories around protected areas? Evidence from fifteen South African National Parks

abstract: Forest landscape restoration (FLR) is central to addressing land degradation, climate change, and rural livelihoods, yet large-scale implementation remains constrained by uncertainty about financial feasibility amid competing land-uses. Existing literature often underrepresents context-specific opportunity costs and cross-scale benefits, limiting the targeting of effective restoration incentives and investments. This study evaluates the financial feasibility of institutional restoration systems (82 forest plantations and 51 Assisted Natural Regeneration (ANR) sites) and farmer-led restoration systems (555 woodlots and 725 agroforestry sites) in Ethiopia, examining how opportunity costs and value-creation options (VCOs) shape economic land-use decisions. We apply a Benefit-Cost Analysis framework to assess four VCOs: technical efficiency improvement, low-interest credit, societal non-market benefits, and carbon credits on financial feasibility. The analysis integrates financial survey data, tree inventories, and contingent valuation per restoration options. Results show that opportunity costs fundamentally shape restoration financial viability and strategy choice. Agroforestry and short-rotation woodlots remain financially viable across contexts, whereas ANR, forest plantations, and mid- to long-rotation woodlots, become non-viable under high opportunity costs. Farm- and communal-level VCOs improve profitability but are generally insufficient to offset delayed returns in long-rotation systems. In contrast, carbon credit VCOs substantially enhance financial viability, particularly for longer investment horizons, although their effectiveness would depend on enabling market and institutional conditions. These findings suggest that restoration policies and investments should be differentiated by local opportunity costs and supported by appropriate tenure and benefit sharing arrangements. By integrating these dimensions, the study provides a scalable decision-support framework for prioritizing restoration investments, targeting incentives, and identifying economically feasible restoration pathways across heterogeneous land-use contexts.
title: Economic feasibility of forest landscape restoration in Ethiopia: Evidence from a multi-scale cost-benefit analysis of institutional and farmer-led systems

abstract: European energy-security analysis has focused mainly on physical supply. This paper examines a less-examined dimension of European energy sovereignty: exposure to the mechanisms through which prices are formed, risks are managed and uncertainty is transmitted across interconnected markets. We distinguish physical dependence on a fuel from exposure to its price, and argue that the combination of weather-driven renewable variability, gas prices and carbon prices is closer to a Keynesian uncertainty than to a sum of insurable risks: their relationships are unstable, policy responses alter the rules of price formation, and hedging can turn price risk into liquidity risk. Nordic annual day-ahead prices for 2015–2025 illustrate the mechanism. In 2022, southern Norway (NO2) and southern Sweden (SE4), with almost no gas-fired generation, averaged €211/MWh and €152/MWh, against €24/MWh (NO4) and €59/MWh (SE1) in the north. This suggests that exposure depends on interconnection and congestion more than on national generation mix, although annual data cannot separate these from hydrology and nuclear availability. Norway and Sweden have since politically responded to this shock by postponing or withdrawing new interconnector investment. We then examine the infrastructure of price formation: Germany's retention of a single bidding zone despite the 2025 Bidding Zone Review, and the concentration of trading, clearing and benchmark functions across electricity, gas and carbon markets notably around EEX Group and ICE. We argue that limiting and distributing this uncertainty, rather than eliminating it, deserves treatment as a dimension of European energy sovereignty alongside security of physical supply.
title: The missing dimension of European energy sovereignty: The geopolitics of market infrastructure

abstract: Employees often work under incomplete contracts, performing both contracted in-role tasks and valuable but noncontracted extra-role activities. Once employees have completed in-role tasks, discretionary time remains, which they may allocate to extra-role activities or consume opportunistically. This study examines how managers’ time-reporting decisions, as a less intrusive form of control, affect subordinates’ effort-allocation decisions. I propose two opposing predictions. First, managers’ control implementations may signal distrust, resulting in more opportunism and thus less extra-role effort. Second, I identify value signaling as a novel theoretical mechanism through which time-reporting decisions may increase extra-role effort. The main experiment manipulated two factors: the type of time report (aggregated versus disaggregated) and its implementation source (managerial choice versus random assignment) to isolate signaling effects from monitoring effects. Results reveal that when managers choose not to implement disaggregated time reporting—that is, reports that make discretionary time salient—subordinates significantly reduce their extra-role effort. Structural equation modeling shows that value signaling outweighs distrust signaling in driving employees’ effort-allocation decisions. In contrast, when the time-reporting format is randomly assigned, effort remains unchanged, underscoring the signaling role of managerial choice. An additional online experiment shows directionally consistent results with the main experiment. These findings reveal a hidden cost of not controlling and contribute to the literature on incomplete contracts, slack resources, and input-based controls in modern work contexts. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Funding: This work was supported by the Bijzonder Onderzoeksfonds UGent [Grant BOF/STA/202009/047]. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00955 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Effortful vs. Opportunistic Consumption of Discretionary Time: How Time-Reporting Decisions Influence Extra-Role Effort

abstract: This paper proposes a data analytics approach for identifying and reducing frictions in digital public service delivery and evaluates its effectiveness in the context of Ethiopia’s 8028 farmer hotline, an interactive voice response (IVR) system for agricultural advice. Guided by funnel analysis identifying IVR menus with high user attrition and by a user survey and focus groups investigating the causes of that attrition, seven system modifications were developed and tested through iterative A/B tests. Three modifications, all of which reduced user hassle, significantly lowered attrition and increased information delivery. The remaining four modifications did not increase information delivery. The most effective intervention addressed friction associated with the collection of user information: removing a multi-step registration process increased access to agricultural advice by 18% without sacrificing valuable user data. In response to these findings, the government ultimately eliminated counterproductive data collection requirements, improving overall system performance. These results demonstrate that data analytics can identify and reduce administrative “sludge” in digital public services and show how data-driven feedback loops can support continuous improvements in government service delivery.
title: De-Sludging digital public service delivery: A data analytics approach

abstract: We construct novel network-based measures of U.S. state-level bank deregulation intensity that allow us to separately identify the effects of deregulation on competition and investment opportunities. In contrast to existing studies, we find that increased competition leads to higher deposit funding costs and a reduction in banks’ net interest margins and profitability. In response, banks shift their business models and persistently increase their risk taking. Our findings resolve conflicting evidence in the literature and support theories in which reductions in bank charter values lead to higher bank risk taking. This paper was accepted by Camelia Kuhnen, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01128 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Deregulation, Market Structure, and the Evolution of U.S. Banking

abstract: This paper explores how venture capitalists (VCs) add value by examining their role as labor market intermediaries. Using novel data, I show that VCs create internal labor markets (ILMs) to facilitate entrepreneurial mobility across their portfolio firms. Survey evidence suggests that VCs leverage private information about founders’ abilities to strategically match talent to portfolio firms, creating value for the recipient companies. Consistent with this mechanism of asymmetric learning, I find that (a) former VC partners continue to influence founder mobility, (b) ILM intensity positively predicts VC fund returns, and (c) the ILM effect is stronger when information asymmetry is greater. This paper was accepted by Lin William Cong, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.01626 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Redeploying the Jockeys: The Intermediary Role of Venture Capital in Entrepreneurial Labor Markets

abstract: Over the past half-century, econometric software has greatly reduced the burden of implementation, while leaving substantive choices about model specification, identification and sample largely to the researcher. Agentic AI can propose specifications and explain their economic rationale, while earlier automated selection methods could simply searched across candidate specifications using statistical criteria. This paper introduces MaRCo@BIS, the MAcroeconometric Research Companion: a framework of plain-text workflow files, a verified dictionary of canonical model specifications and a tested reference library, read by an off-the-shelf agentic coding environment. MaRCo@BIS proposes specifications and provides their rationale, retrieves and harmonises data, estimates, checks results against economic priors and logs every choice for replication, while the researcher confirms or overrides each (consequential) decision. We document the design, benchmark the agent’s replications of three widely-used structural VARs against the originals, and illustrate the framework across five exercises ranging from a verified replication to an open design question. We also discuss the necessity of human supervision, the risks of specification search and automation bias, and the safeguards against these risks. The framework is released as a public good for the central banking community and macroeconomic researchers more broadly.
title: MaRCo@BIS: AI-agentic econometric analysis for central bankers

abstract: This study contributes to the debate on how government spending shapes the growth process. We take the analysis in three new directions. First, we consider government spending, both as a flow and as a cumulated stock, in a scale-invariant Schumpeterian model of endogenous innovation. Second, we allow public spending to be the catalyst that precipitates an industrial takeoff. Third, we postulate a production structure that generates robust endogenous growth by violating the conventional condition for endogenous growth, namely, that the economy’s reduced-form production function must be linear in the accumulated factor. With non-distortionary taxation, increasing productive government spending causes an earlier industrial takeoff and faster economic growth. With distortionary labor-income tax under elastic labor supply, instead, increasing productive government spending has a U-shaped effect on the timing of the industrial takeoff and an inverted-U effect on economic growth. Using cross-country panel data, we document a hump-shaped relationship between productive government spending and economic growth. Calibrating the model to the UK and the US, we find that raising productive government spending from its historical value to its growth-maximizing value causes an earlier industrial takeoff by over two decades and an increase in the long-run level of output by about 40% in both cases. We also explore the robustness of our results under a consumption tax and a corporate income tax.
title: Paving the road to prosperity: Productive government spending, takeoff and robust endogenous growth

abstract: Since the liberalization of European electricity markets in the late 1990s, many aspects of the energy landscape have changed significantly. In this study, we investigate how the day-ahead electricity market has developed over time and how these changes are related to the growth of renewable generation, changes in fossil fuel prices and increased international integration. We do this using a rich dataset from the European Power Exchange, containing data on hourly bids that were submitted in the Dutch day-ahead market in the period 2006–2024. We use these bids to construct demand and supply curves, estimate the price elasticities of demand and supply from these curves, and examine how these elasticities have evolved over time in response to the above-mentioned developments. Our results show that both elasticities have decreased over time. The decrease in elasticities of demand is related to the growth in renewable electricity supply, as renewable production changes the number of bids and the distribution of bid prices. Supply curves are affected by renewable production via the same mechanisms, but these mechanisms now work in opposite directions such that there is no clear relationship between between renewable production and elasticities of supply. We also find that increased international trade is associated with lower elasticities as supply and demand curves shift, while the relationship between fuel prices and elasticities is less consistent.
title: How energy system developments affect elasticities in day-ahead electricity markets: Evidence from bid curves

abstract: This paper examines the effects of flow-based market coupling and renewable electricity generation on price convergence and transmission patterns in the Scandinavian electricity market. Using hourly day-ahead data for the Norwegian bidding zones NO1 and NO2 and the Danish bidding zone DK1 from January 2023 to September 2025, we estimate fixed-effects panel regressions to analyze how the introduction of Flow-Based Market Coupling (FBMC) in October 2024 affected cross-border and internal market integration. The results show that FBMC is associated with improved price convergence and higher exports between NO2 and DK1, while its direct effect on internal Norwegian price convergence and transmission between NO2 and NO1 is limited. Renewable generation remains an important driver of market outcomes, with Danish wind generation continuing to widen cross-border price differences and Norwegian renewable generation playing a stronger role in supporting cross-border exchange after the reform. Overall, the findings suggest that FBMC can improve aspects of market integration, but that its effectiveness depends on underlying generation patterns, network constraints, and complementary grid capacity and flexibility resources. This highlights the importance of combining market-design reforms with grid reinforcement and flexibility measures as renewable penetration increases.
title: Flow-based market coupling and market integration in the Nordic electricity market: Evidence from price convergence and transmission

abstract: Governments increasingly use financial incentives to promote electric and hybrid vehicles, yet evidence on their effects on urban air quality remains limited. This paper studies sub-national vehicle incentives in Italian provincial capital municipalities over 2013–2023. Exploiting spatial and temporal variation in regional, autonomous-provincial, and municipal policies, we implement a staggered-adoption difference-in-differences design accounting for heterogeneous treatment timing. We distinguish between direct cash subsidies, which reduce the upfront purchase price, and fiscal incentives operating through vehicle-tax exemptions or reductions. In our preferred specification, exposure to policy environments including cash subsidies reduces the maximum annual average concentration of nitrogen dioxide (NO2) by about 2.5 μ g/m 3 , or 8.3 percent of the sample mean. The effect develops gradually after adoption and remains robust across alternative comparison cohorts and additional checks. By contrast, pooled and fiscal specifications provide no comparable evidence of improved air quality, while the fiscal event studies exhibit differential pre-treatment dynamics. Cash-incentive exposure is also followed by a delayed increase in electric and hybrid vehicles and a decline in the diesel component of the passenger-car fleet. The effect of local incentive programs are less clear in terms of gasoline car purchases. Overall, measurable improvements in urban air quality are more clearly identified in policy environments including upfront subsidies.
title: Clean vehicle incentive design and urban air quality: Evidence from Italy

abstract: Energy vulnerability has far-reaching consequences for economic performance, climate resilience, and environmental sustainability. This study provides empirical evidence on how artificial intelligence (AI) innovation, green investments (GI), and energy balance (EB) can be used to reduce energy vulnerability. Using data from 2000 to 2022 and a combination of panel econometric and machine learning (ML) techniques, the study examines the effects of these factors on energy vulnerability across the G10 economies. It also evaluates the moderating roles of energy efficiency, energy transition, energy intensity, and governance quality. The findings show that AI has a limited vulnerability-reducing effect when the G10 countries are considered collectively. At the country level, however, AI significantly lowers energy vulnerability in Denmark, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom. It also reduces energy vulnerability marginally in the remaining G10 economies, except Sweden, where its effect is positive and substantial. GI significantly lowers energy vulnerability in France, Japan, and the United States, while EB produces a significant reduction only in the Netherlands. The effects of GI and EB vary across other G10 countries, highlighting the need for country-specific policy responses. Results from the best-performing machine learning model, Gradient Boosting, reveal that AI is the most influential predictor of energy vulnerability. It is followed by energy efficiency, energy transition, and green investment. Based on these findings, policymakers should encourage the use of supervised AI in grid management and energy systems to limit the adverse effects associated with AI-driven energy demand. Additional measures include developing real-time vulnerability assessment metrics for green investment projects and linking energy balance to electricity tariffs through time-of-use pricing mechanisms.
title: Strategies to minimize energy vulnerability: A machine learning assessment of the roles of artificial intelligence innovations, green investments, and energy balance

abstract: Ferrara (2026) shows economic historians how to use large language models to turn historical sources into data. His guide sets out an iterative workflow, from describing a task to validating the result, and applies it in four worked examples: emotions in paintings, name-blind census linking, newspaper sentiment around the Chinese Exclusion Act and the delivery of Roosevelt’s wartime speeches. I extend this account of data production to the rest of the research process. As processing becomes cheap for everyone, the advantage of being able to perform it dissipates and scarcity shifts to choosing questions and interpreting evidence. Models also change quickly. The median article in recent issues of Explorations in Economic History saw five model release announcements between submission and acceptance, making the organisation and documentation of research a recurring decision. Cheaper processing allows researchers to test more questions, read whole corpora and turn neglected archives into public history resources. On writing, I argue that an author must answer for the argument but need not produce every sentence. The risks include errors entering later training data, unequal access and pressure on peer review. Training will have to change as some skills lose value and others gain it. How new entrants acquire the skills that complement these tools is perhaps the most pressing question the discipline now faces.

abstract: This paper studies horizontal mergers in a production network. I show that greater downstream centrality – the extent to which other sectors rely, directly or indirectly, on a sector’s output – reduces the cost synergy required for a merger to be pro-competitive when final-demand elasticity exceeds the elasticity of substitution in production.
title: Centrality as a merger defense

abstract: We address the systemic risk-driven portfolio optimization problem using two nonparametric methods: Sample Average Approximation (SAA) and Performance-Based Regularization (PBR). Both methods rely on empirical estimators and do not make distributional assumptions. We investigate the asymptotic properties of the solutions within the Conditional Expected Shortfall (CoES) optimization framework. When applied to portfolios constructed separately using the three Fama–French data sets, these methods demonstrate improved risk-adjusted returns during market downturns in two of the three.
title: Nonparametric systemic risk-driven portfolio selection

abstract: I show that the two-level nested logit model arises exactly from a sequential choice process in which group, subgroup, and product shocks are revealed in stages. The result extends to any number of levels and holds for any nesting parameters below one, without the bounds and ordering that random utility maximization requires. Parameter estimates that applied work discards for violating the standard ordering or the lower bound are consistent with sequential choice. The linear inversion and welfare formula hold. When the standard ordering fails, improving one product can raise a rival's market share in its subgroup, even with single-unit demand.
title: A sequential foundation for two-level nested logit

abstract: We study a model of persuasion in which the receiver's updating rule systematically distorts Bayesian posteriors. While in the classic Bayesian case providing information sequentially is never valuable, we show that the sender gains from sequential persuasion in several of the environments considered in the literature on strategic information transmission. Our proofs are constructive and reveal how properties of the bias interact with the payoff environment to make dynamic persuasion beneficial.
title: Sequential Non-Bayesian Persuasion

abstract: The utilization of automation in recent decades and its displacement effect on routine tasks is well documented, but its further influence on market structure has not been studied. In this paper, we analyze micro panel data for manufacturing in China from 2013-2020 and suggest how the adoption of automation influences markup divergence through routine tasks. We find that (i) automation raises markups for firms; (ii) firms contain more routine tasks benefit more from automation for their markups; (iii) the difference in markups between high and low markup firms increases because high markup firms which already perform better can import more automation machines to substitute workers doing routine tasks. The results still hold after mitigating endogeneity and implementing a series of robustness tests.

abstract: Using a novel setting, we examine auditors’ responses to public warnings of audit risk and whether their nonresponses are associated with auditor and client characteristics. We focus on 243 short-selling campaigns from 2006 to 2020 in which short sellers make public, credible allegations of audit-related issues against listed companies. Of those companies’ auditors, 48.3% do not take any observable actions in terms of raising audit fees substantially, terminating the engagement, issuing going concern opinions, or reporting internal control weaknesses in the year after the short sellers’ allegations. We further find that longer auditor–client tenure is the factor most consistently associated with auditors’ nonresponse to public warnings of audit risk, a pattern arguably consistent with impaired independence. Additional analyses show that the litigation and reputation costs of auditors’ inactions are minimal, further reducing auditors’ incentives for responses.
title: Auditors’ (non)responses to public warnings of audit risk: evidence from short-selling campaigns

abstract: Postal and courier services have become an important channel for drug trafficking worldwide. This study examines the impact of digital monitoring of mail on drug use. Based on the universe of drug arrest records in a populous province in China, the difference-in-differences analysis reveals that, after the implementation of real-identity mailing (RIM) in 2017, the number of punished drug users decreased by 5.8% in townships with any courier service points. This effect persists for at least 1 year. The number of first-time users diminishes, while the number of addicted users remains constant. These suggest that strengthening the regulation of postal and courier services may be a cost-effective approach to drug control, and courier service platforms and government could collaborate to solve public health challenges and improve social welfare.

abstract: The quality of investors’ information across different horizons has real effects. When managers care about the effect of investment on their stock price, a decline in the informativeness of investors’ signals about long-term cash flows leads firms with long-term projects to cut investment more than firms with short-term projects. Using a novel, hand-collected measure of project horizons, we confirm this hypothesis: relative to firms with short-term projects, the investment of firms with long-term projects decreases by 3.7% following a 1-standard-deviation drop in the quality of investors’ long-term information. This effect becomes larger when managers prioritize current stock prices. (JEL D84, G14, G17, M41).
title: The Horizon of Investors’ Information and Corporate Investment

abstract: A central puzzle in the social sciences is that, despite high and rising inequality, democracies consistently under-deliver redistributive policies. Research in economics and political science has documented one explanation for this puzzle: beliefs about the extent of inequality are polarized along ideological lines, with liberals believing there to be more inequality than conservatives. We decompose this ideological divide in inequality perceptions into two sources: the decision threshold applied by liberals and conservatives when classifying possible instances of inequality (‘criterion’) and their tendency to perceive inequality to begin with (‘sensitivity’). Across six studies (N = 2734), we find that liberals consistently report seeing more inequality than conservatives when exposed to identical stimuli. A formal signal detection decomposition reveals ideological differences in both the discriminability of inequality signals (‘sensitivity’) and the threshold applied when classifying them (‘criterion’). The ideological gap in perceived inequality disappears when stimuli depict inequality unambiguously— that is, when the signal is strong enough to clear even the strictest decision thresholds. Notably, we find that perceived inequality is associated with fairness concerns and support for redistributive policies above and beyond ideological orientation. These findings suggest that the everyday settings in which people encounter instances of social inequality are themselves likely to produce consequential differences in beliefs about the extent of inequality.
journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
source_issue: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 252
title: Decomposing the ideological divide in perceptions of inequality: a signal detection approach

abstract: This paper studies the effect of regional trade agreements on firms’ exports using detailed information on the content of trade agreements and firm-level exports for 31 developing countries between 2000 and 2020. Moving from shallow to deep trade agreements—-i.e. agreements that regulate border and behind-the-border policies—-boosts firms’ exports, on average, by 3.6 percent. This effect is stronger for large firms and firms involved in global value chains and (weakly) negative for small firms, documenting a reallocation of exports toward larger exporters associated with deeper agreements—consistent with models of trade with heterogeneous firms—with significant welfare consequences for signatory countries. An Instrumental Variable strategy and a battery of robustness tests confirm the causal interpretation of the results.
title: Deep trade agreements and heterogeneous firms’ exports

abstract: 城乡融合发展是中国式现代化的必然要求，对于推进乡村全面振兴、实现共同富裕具有重要意义。现有相关研究多局限于经济学、社会学、管理学等单一学科视角，对城乡复合生态系统的整体属性关注不足，生态维度的研究存在明显短板，难以系统解释城乡生态割裂的深层机理与破解路径。本文以共生理论、生态位理论、稳定性理论、演替理论、平衡理论这五大生态学理论为支撑，构建城乡融合发展的递进式分析框架，阐释了城乡复合生态系统从失衡走向共生、从低级向高级演化的内在机理。在此基础上，结合生态学核心原理，从筑牢城乡融合发展的生态基底、构建差异化发展格局、提升系统抗风险能力、推动阶梯式演进、实现公平共享五个维度，提出了具有可操作性的实践策略，涵盖了生态空间管控、物质循环利用、功能冗余保障、产业梯度升级、要素双向流动、公共服务均等化及生态保护补偿机制等重点领域。本文突破传统研究范式，将生态学理论体系有机融入城乡融合发展研究之中，拓展生态规律与城乡关系系统性结合的研究视角，以期为破解城乡二元结构、修复城乡生态割裂、构建城乡生态共生体系提供理论支撑与实践参考，对推进人与自然和谐共生的中国式现代化具有重要价值。

abstract: 在中国区域和城乡收入差距仍然较大的情况下，核心劳动年龄群体的流动却在快速下降，传统经济模型遭遇解释困境。本文揭示子女升学压力已成为束缚劳动力流动的一个重要因素。结合当前教育竞争加剧的现实背景，本文构建包含子女升学压力的家庭流动决策模型，运用2005－2015年全国人口普查抽样微观数据与2023年中国住户收入调查（CHIP）数据，借助工具变量法检验子女升学压力对劳动力流动的影响及其机制。研究发现，子女升学压力会显著抑制劳动力流动，且对升学压力更大、教育期望更高以及社会经济资源相对有限的家庭影响更为突出。机制分析表明，子女升学压力迫使父母增加照料时间，同时因担心留守子女发展而承受较高的心理成本，从而削弱了流动意愿。进一步讨论显示，子女升学压力更多抑制远距离跨省流动，但降低迁入地落户门槛可有效缓解这一负向效应。本文揭示了教育竞争对劳动力流动的梗阻效应，应通过提升随迁子女教育保障水平、缩小区域教育资源差距、增强职业教育吸引力，助推劳动力要素高效配置。

abstract: 深化县域医疗卫生服务体系改革、开展县域医疗卫生共同体建设，既是落实健康中国战略的重要举措，也是减轻居民就医负担的有效途径。本文利用2014－2022年中国家庭追踪调查（CFPS）数据，运用交错双重差分法，考察县域医疗卫生共同体建设对居民就医负担的影响及其作用机制。研究发现，县域医疗卫生共同体建设显著减少了居民自付医疗费用，且减负效应主要集中于高额自付医疗费用群体；机制分析表明，县域医疗卫生共同体建设通过提升医疗服务质量和降低居民患病风险两条路径减轻居民就医负担；异质性分析显示，县域医疗卫生共同体建设对基期首诊机构选择为高层级医疗机构和基期健康状况较差居民的就医负担减轻效应更为显著，而参与不同医保类型的居民之间的就医负担减轻效应未表现出显著差异。本文从减轻居民就医负担的角度揭示了县域医疗卫生共同体建设的政策效应及其作用机制，以期为全面推进县域医疗卫生共同体建设、深入实施健康中国战略提供经验证据和政策启示。

abstract: 本文立足中国“大国小农”的基本国情农情与农业现代化实践，着眼农业新质生产力发展的时代背景，聚焦农业的自然依赖性及其分工约束问题，对“斯密判断”所揭示的农业分工受限这一经典命题进行重新审视。研究表明，农业新质生产力以生物技术、数字技术和智能装备等前沿技术的突破为基础，经由技术革命、要素重构与组织创新三重路径，系统性地弱化农业在空间、时间与过程上的自然依赖性，从而为打破传统的“自然－小农”双重锁定结构提供物质基础和技术条件。这一弱化自然依赖性的生产力质变，推动农业生产关系在经营模式、产权结构、产业形态与治理体系四个维度发生深刻重构，并由此形成以服务规模化和数字网络化赋能小农为特征的中国农业现代化路径。本文提出的“自然依赖性弱化”命题及其分析框架，为理解农业生产关系重构提供了新的理论视角，也为中国农业现代化实践提供了学理依据与政策启示。

abstract: 农产品期货交易形成的价格信号能够汇集并传递分散于不同地区的市场信息，为缓解区域间信息不对称创造条件。本文使用中国89家大型农副产品批发市场的100余万条日度价格数据，采用动态价格法测算11种农产品在城市配对层面的季度市场一体化指标，并将农产品期货上市视为准自然实验，采用双重差分法考察其对现货市场一体化的影响。研究发现：第一，农产品期货上市提高了对应农产品的现货市场一体化水平，促进信息整合与加快信息传导是其重要作用机制。第二，农产品期货市场流动性的改善和套期保值交易活跃度的提高均有助于促进现货市场一体化。第三，在地理距离较远的城市之间，农产品期货上市与高铁连通具有协同促进现货市场一体化的作用。本文研究结论有助于理解期货市场对农产品区域间价格差异的影响，并为推进全国统一大市场建设提供经验证据。

abstract: 本文以中国、美国、巴西、阿根廷和加拿大五国大豆市场为样本，采用分位数时频溢出指数方法，系统测度主要贸易伙伴国与中国大豆市场间的价格溢出效应，进而实证探究气候风险对大豆价格跨境溢出的影响及作用渠道。研究发现：第一，主要贸易伙伴国与中国大豆市场间存在较强的价格溢出效应；正常状态下的总溢出水平低于极端状态，短期溢出强于长期溢出。第二，大豆价格跨境溢出网络中的主导国随市场状态动态调整。第三，无论是在何种市场状态和时间频率下，中国始终是溢出效应的净输入方。第四，贸易伙伴国气候风险上升会加剧其对中国大豆市场的价格溢出效应。其中，气候物理风险的影响具有常态化趋势，主要通过国际贸易渠道传导；气候转型风险的影响更多反映在极端市场状态下，主要通过情绪传染渠道传导。第五，气候风险对大豆价格跨境溢出的影响具有显著的区域异质性，南美国家为价格极端下跌状态下气候物理风险向中国长期传导的核心来源地；北美国家既主导了气候物理风险对中国大豆价格的常态化传导，也是价格极端上涨状态下气候转型风险向中国长期传导的核心来源地。本文研究为防范外部气候风险冲击、维护国内大豆市场稳定以及保障国家粮食安全提供了有益启示。

abstract: 政策性农业信贷担保作为破解农村融资约束的重要政策工具，对粮食生产中的环境友好、增产增收具有重要的赋能作用。本文以2015年起中国各地级市逐步设立政策性农业信贷担保分支机构作为政策冲击，运用多时期双重差分模型考察政策性农业信贷担保对粮食可持续生产能力的影响及作用机制。研究表明：政策性农业信贷担保对粮食可持续生产能力具有显著的提升作用。促进信贷供给下沉和推动农业资本深化是两个重要的影响机制。不同于政策性农业信贷担保只要释放效能便会带动信贷供给下沉的作用逻辑，随着时间的推移，政策性农业信贷担保对粮食生产中农业资本深化的推动作用呈逐渐减弱趋势，这主要源于“去担保化”的影响。此外，政策性农业信贷担保更有助于提高粮食主产区、财政涉农支持程度低和数字金融水平低的地区的粮食可持续生产能力。本文建议，提高担保的精准覆盖度与服务可得性，推动“去担保化”平稳过渡并构建长效服务机制，实施区域差异化支持政策，进而推动农业信贷担保政策高效落地。

abstract: 农村集体经济组织在传统经营中面临市场竞争能力弱、治理不完善等诸多问题，设立公司被视为盘活集体资源、发展新型农村集体经济的重要举措。然而，实践中农村集体经济组织如何成功设立公司仍是有待研究的重要问题。本文采用多案例研究方法，选取四个典型村庄，深入探究农村集体经济组织设立公司的差异化路径及其选择依据。研究发现，基于参与主体的不同，实践中主要形成了单村独立运营、多村抱团、村企合作以及与自然人合资四条有效路径。不同路径具有各自的适用条件：单村独立运营适用于具备潜在资源优势且内部组织有力的村庄；多村抱团适用于地域相邻、具备一定资源且上级政府能够有效统筹的村庄集群；村企合作适用于开发潜力较大但缺乏资本与运营能力的村庄；与自然人合资则适用于具备资源优势、拟开发中小型项目的村庄。同时，各条路径在实践中均面临一定的潜在风险。本文拓展了产权理论的研究边界，为发展壮大新型农村集体经济、推进乡村振兴与实现共同富裕提供了理论参考和路径选择。

abstract: 盘活农村集体经营性资产，是发展壮大新型农村集体经济和扎实推进乡村全面振兴的重要抓手。本文基于2020－2022年中国土地经济调查数据，从利益联结视角出发，分析村庄产业融合对村集体经营性资产价值实现的影响及其作用机制，并识别风险治理的边界条件。研究表明：第一，村庄产业融合显著促进了村集体经营性资产价值实现，主要体现在内部融合型与多功能拓展型两种产业融合模式的发展上。第二，村庄产业融合通过土地集中流转、强化农户集体行动、吸引社会资本投资以及建立利益联结共享机制等方式促进村集体经营性资产价值实现。第三，有效契约和组织监管作为风险治理的关键边界条件，有助于防范村庄产业融合过程中的契约风险，保障村集体经营性资产价值实现的安全性与稳定性。第四，上述效应在基础设施更加完善、治理能力更强的村庄中更为显著；相较于单一的“合作社”或“龙头企业”模式，“合作社+龙头企业”模式是实现村集体经营性资产价值的更优组织形式。上述结论为推进农村产业融合发展，进而盘活农村集体经营性资产、壮大新型农村集体经济提供了微观证据与决策参考。

abstract: Can artificial intelligence extend students’ analytical capabilities without displacing their independent judgement? This column reports on a pilot study in a graduate seminar investigating weaknesses in European integration. An ‘AI-enriched contract’ required three elements for students’ presentations: an independent conceptualisation before AI use, an AI-assisted presentation, and a transparency statement. AI-tools accelerated routine execution, widened methodological ambition, and enabled exploration. Students also documented verification, rejected inappropriate suggestions and fabricated quotations, and retained responsibility for organisation and interpretation of findings. While the pilot offers qualified support for AI as a workmate rather than a master, several caveats apply.
title: AI – Master and Commander: Lessons from graduate student projects and the need for an AI-enriched contract

abstract: Official statistics are getting harder to collect and can arrive late. This column uses generative AI to read managers’ economic outlooks from more than 120,000 corporate earnings calls in the US. The resulting score predicts GDP, employment, and wages beyond the next quarter and carries information that professional forecasters do not.
authors: Manish Jha, Jialin Qian, Michael Weber, Baozhong Yang
title: Reading the economy from earnings calls with generative AI

abstract: Despite climate-mitigation commitments in the global South, an implementation gap constrains sustainable agricultural development in South Africa. This study examines government extension practitioners' perceptions of climate-aligned practices to identify the institutional factors driving this divide. A qualitative content analysis of 1775 thematic segments from focus groups with 52 extension officers across eight provinces in 2025 reveals deep institutional misalignment. Only 10.7% of coded segments explicitly framed agriculture as a mitigation strategy, while 35.8% prioritize economic optimization and livelihood conservation. Provincial focus on climate mitigation ranges from 20.3% in Mpumalanga to 4.7% in Gauteng. Crucially, land tenure insecurity emerges as a foundational structural constraint that contributes to this misalignment by discouraging long-term climate investment. While national mandates conceptualize mitigation through global carbon accounting, local extension systems prioritize immediate economic survival. Therefore, achieving national targets requires reforming communal land governance alongside extension mandates, rather than merely introducing technical solutions. The study demonstrates that land governance reform is a prerequisite, rather than a complementary measure, for effective climate policy implementation. It advances frameworks that leverage smart technologies for carbon measurement, youth-led data management, and carbon credits, reframing mitigation as a viable economic strategy for a sustainable, low-carbon future.
title: Transitioning to low-carbon agriculture: Institutional misalignment and constraints in South Africa’s extension systems

abstract: Urbanization and associated land use and land cover (LULC) change are major drivers of surface transformation with significant implications for climate impacts. The conversion of vegetated and permeable landscapes into built-up areas alters energy balance, disrupts carbon and hydrological cycles, and intensifies heat exposure. However, existing studies remain fragmented, with most studies examining urbanization, LULC change, or climate impacts separately, without fully integrating them into a unified framework. To address this gap, this study provides a comprehensive global synthesis of the interactions among urbanization, LULC change, and climate impacts. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, the review synthesizes 116 peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2024 that examine urban expansion, LULC transitions, and climate-related outcomes. The results show that urban growth is predominantly driven by peri-urban expansion, with the conversion of vegetated land to impervious surfaces emerging as the dominant land transition. The reviewed studies further indicate that the climate impacts of urbanization and associated LULC change extend beyond rising land surface temperatures to include changes in energy balance, hydrological processes, and carbon dynamics. The findings have important implications for integrated land-use planning and zoning, compact urban development, urban greening, and coordinated planning aimed at moderating the climatic impacts of urban expansion. However, existing planning responses may remain insufficient in many rapidly urbanizing contexts, highlighting the need for stronger implementation and better coordination to support climate-resilient and sustainable urban development.
title: Understanding interactions among urbanization, land use and land cover change, and climate impacts: Implications for climate-resilient urban planning

abstract: Technical innovations that remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere are gaining attention to compensate for the insufficient pace of emissions reductions. Given the scale of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) deployment envisioned, there is a notable deficit in our understanding of the underlying predictors of public support of CDR, particularly in the global South. In economic theory, risk, time and social preferences serve as fundamental predictors of judgment and decision making. The current article thus undertakes a systematic examination of economic preferences and how they predict support for three CDR technologies (direct air capture, enhanced rock weathering, afforestation and reforestation). We employ experimentally validated instruments to examine how fundamental differences in individual tendencies to take risks, be patient or act pro-socially affect CDR support. Drawing on nationally representative surveys in five countries ( n = 4000 respondents from Brazil, China, Germany, Kenya, USA), we first establish how CDR support varies between technologies and countries, with support lower for novel CDR technologies and broadly higher for global South publics. To explain such differences, we reveal the relevance of economic preferences for CDR support, notably the positive predictive effects of risk-taking, altruism, and trust. We also indicate how the relevance of economic preferences varies across technologies and countries. Risk-taking, altruism and trust have stronger effects on novel, engineered CDR support, but positive reciprocity matters more for afforestation. The results stress the importance of economic preferences as core, under-explored predictors of individual and cross-country variation in public support of CDR technologies.

abstract: This paper studies monetary policy in the presence of temporary, sector-level supply bottlenecks within a rich production-network framework. We first show that binding sectoral constraints steepen the aggregate supply curve and alter the inflation-output trade-off when they interact with shifts in demand. Our main contribution is to show that the temporary nature of these constraints creates an additional intertemporal policy trade-off. Monetary policy actions while constraints bind affect sectoral relative prices, which may adjust only gradually and may no longer be appropriate once constraints ease. Policy therefore faces a trade-off between stabilizing the economy during the constrained period and limiting the relative-price adjustment required afterwards. We study these mechanisms in a calibrated two-region, multi-sector New Keynesian model with production networks and heterogeneous price stickiness. Production complementarities and heterogeneous price adjustment can amplify or attenuate sectoral shocks as they propagate through the network. We fit the model to data from 2020--2024 and find that supply constraints contributed substantially to U.S. inflation and dampened the output response to demand during the pandemic recovery. Counterfactual analysis shows that accounting for binding constraints makes monetary tightening more effective in reducing inflation and less costly in terms of output. We also find that coordinated tightening across regions mitigates inflation spillovers transmitted through global production networks.
authors: Galip Kemal Ozhan & Nick Sander & Sebastian Wende & Sihwan Yang
title: Monetary Policy Under Network-Level Bottlenecks

abstract: We develop a flexible methodology for estimating a real-time term structure of inflation expectations from heterogeneous survey- and market-based sources. Our Nelson-Siegel Internally Consistent Expectations model extends the standard dynamic Nelson-Siegel state-space model by imposing a restriction that forecasts of any fixed-horizon event are revised only in response to new information, and by calibrating measurement-error variances to each source’s historical forecast accuracy. The resulting composite summarizes expectations at all horizons in a single internally-consistent term structure that can be applied in a variety of contexts, including when data sources are reported at irregular intervals and horizons. To illustrate our framework, we apply the model to Japanese inflation expectations data, and document a gradual alignment of long-run inflation expectations with the Bank of Japan’s 2-percent target from below.
authors: Mr. Yan Carriere-Swallow & Jason Lu & Mr. Ken Teoh
title: A Flexible Composite Term Structure of Inflation Expectations

abstract: Quarterly Projection Models (QPMs) are widely used at central banks but rarely estimated by full Bayesian methods, because rational-expectations solvers and shock-variance priors resist gradient-based inference. We develop a workf low pairing the structure-preserving doubling algorithm, automatic dif ferentiation and the No-U-Turn Sampler with a signal-to-noise-ratio prior calibration refined by a Koopman disturbance-smoother EM step. Applied to an open-economy QPM for Brazil (2004Q1–2025Q2), it delivers stable posterior inference, tightens monetary-policy impulse-response bands relative to the prior, places the output gap inside the Banco Central do Brasil’s published envelope in about 84% of the sample, and produces stable pseudo-real-time forecasts, with its clearest edge over a Bayesian VAR on the policy rate.

abstract: This paper quantifies the macro-fiscal consequences of geoeconomic fragmentation using the Geopolitical Fragmentation Index of Fernández Villaverde, Mineyama, and Song (2024). Using a panel of 90 economies over 1990−2022, we identify structural fragmentation shocks in a panel SVAR and trace their dynamic effects through local projections, allowing for heterogeneity across country groups. We find that a one standard deviation increase in geoeconomic fragmentation raises public debt by up to 3 percentage points of GDP in the medium term. The debt buildup reflects weaker economic activity, wider fiscal deficits driven by higher spending and lower revenues, and a temporary tightening of financing conditions. The effects are stronger in advanced economies and in countries more exposed to geopolitically distant trade partners. Geoeconomic fragmentation also amplifies uncertainty around future debt and growth and increases the risk of tail events.

abstract: Securities lending – the temporary transfer of securities in exchange for collateral – is essential to the modern financial system, facilitating short selling, market making, and efficient liquidity management. Yet, little is known about how these contracts are priced. Using comprehensive transaction-level data, we identify the determinants of returns from lending the same security against cash or securities collateral. We develop a model in which lending returns compensate for security risk, illiquidity, and the use of scarce dealer balance-sheet capacity. We also define a return wedge between the two market segments. Consistent with the model, the wedge widens with risk, illiquidity, dealer constraints, and collateral reusability but narrows as participation across both segments increases.
authors: Evangelos Benos & Gerardo Ferrara & Angelo Ranaldo & Vittorio Vergano
title: Price efficiency in securities lending

abstract: This study evaluates ten priority research areas for advancing understanding of economic exploitation and inequality, encompassing conceptual and methodological challenges, technological transformations, labour market developments, structural disadvantages, institutional arrangements and the effectiveness of policy interventions. It introduces the Journal of Economic Exploitation and Inequality (JOEEI) as an international scholarly forum committed to addressing these challenges through theoretical, empirical and interdisciplinary inquiry. Drawing on diverse traditions of economic thought, the editorial examines the relationships between exploitation, inequality, economic power and institutional practices, emphasising the importance of conceptual clarity, methodological rigour and intellectual pluralism. It also reviews the six articles published in the inaugural issue, considering their contributions to contemporary debates and their connections to the journal's wider research agenda. The discussion highlights how structural conditions, institutional arrangements and individual behaviour may shape exploitative relationships and unequal economic outcomes across different contexts.
title: Advancing the Study of Economic Exploitation and Inequality: Introducing a New Scholarly Forum

abstract: Paid domestic care is an important part of ageing-at-home policies, yet it competes with other household needs for limited resources. We estimate a two-stage demand system using the Italian Household Budget Survey for 2014–2023, focusing on households with at least one member aged 65 or over. The first stage allocates total expenditure across broad consumption categories; the second divides the health-and-care budget among medical services, health products and paid domestic care. Health-and-care expenditure rises more than proportionally with total expenditure, and domestic care is the most expenditure-responsive component within that budget. The linked expenditure elasticity is 1.678. Demand among existing domestic-care purchasers is also price elastic. With a 10 per cent reduction in the consumer price, their quantity purchased rises by 29.9 per cent, while predicted participation increases by 7.4 percentage points in the lower-block population. The quartile simulations suggest a stronger participation response among lower-expenditure households. These results distinguish support for existing users from access to paid care and suggest a role for affordability, and indicate that demand for paid care is responsive to policy.
title: Paying for Care: Household Budgets and Domestic Care in Italy

abstract: We study whether children’s behavior changes when caregivers delegate a decision to them. Running an experiment with 956 caregiver-child pairs in Thailand, we let caregivers either retain decision rights or delegate them to children across four incentivized tasks covering time, risk, competitive, and social preferences. We find domain-specific effects of delegation. Delegation makes children more patient, but we find no effects on risk, competitive and social preferences. A simple theoretical framework can rationalize this pattern, as it predicts delegation to affect behavior most when caregivers’ and children’s preferences diverge substantially, as is primarily the case in the time-preference task.
title: Delegation and Children’s Decision-Making: Evidence from Thailand

abstract: We evaluate a guaranteed basic income experiment providing twelve monthly $500 transfers to very low-income US households. During the final month of payments, a survey index of financial distress declined by 0.18 SD, and an overall well-being index increased by 0.15 SD. By contrast, collections balances from credit reports show no change during transfers and likely increase for some recipients in the year after transfers end. These results appear to be driven by changes in financial decision-making including shifts away from informal borrowing and toward future returns.
title: How Temporary Cash Transfers Affect Household Finances

abstract: Despite pregnancy-focused public insurance coverage in the U.S., low-income mothers and infants face persistent health disadvantages. Using linked birth, tax, and enrollment data, we examine the effects of preconception coverage from California's 2014 Medicaid expansion, comparing changes in outcomes for first-time mothers just below and above the income eligibility threshold. Expansion increased preconception Medicaid enrollment by 3.4 months (+23 percentage points in 12-month continuous coverage), first-month pregnancy enrollment by 24 percentage points, and adequate prenatal care and STI screening. Yet we find no improvements in maternal or infant health, suggesting preconception coverage alone cannot close health disparities.
title: Preconception Medicaid and Maternal and Infant Health: Evidence from Linked Administrative Data

abstract: In decentralized school systems where core funding comes from local governments, the central government sometimes provides grants on top of the core funding (e.g. Title I in the US). In Sweden, such grants have grown from around 3 of compulsory school costs in 2010 to 7% in 2023. For the grants to have an impact, providers must claim their entitlements which requires submitting a detailed plan for fund usage and not all providers do this, especially not smaller private providers. We study how the size of the grant entitlement affects providers’ take-up decisions. This is a margin that readily can be adjusted by e.g. merging smaller grants to a single larger. We exploit variation from a large grant in Sweden that allocated substantially more money to providers with a socioeconomic student composition below a certain threshold value. Using a regression discontinuity design, we find that take-up among private providers increased from 70% to 88% as the grant amount increased from about 4% to 13% of the total cost per student. Importantly, the effect on take-up appears to be sticky as it remains in a later year when the compensatory part was removed from the grant and all providers were entitled to the same amount per student.
title: Education Providers’ Take-Up of Government Grants: Evidence from a Grant Allocation Discontinuity

abstract: Forced sterilization represents one of several coercive population control measures enacted during the 20th century. This paper examines the short- and long-run effects of coerced sterilization, drawing evidence from the experience of Native American women in the 1970s. Beyond reduced fertility, our findings indicate that, in the long run, Native American women exposed to forced sterilization experienced worse health outcomes, lower labor market participation, lower income, and decreased investment in their children’s education. We also examine the intergenerational transmission of fertility choices and find suggestive evidence of a reversal: children of mothers exposed to forced sterilization have higher fertility.
title: The Effects of Coerced Sterilization: Evidence from Native American Women

abstract: We study whether financial assistance to prospective homebuyers succeeds in promoting homeownership by analyzing a prominent real-estate transfer tax exemption for young homebuyers in the Netherlands. The reform offers quasi-experimental variation across time, buyers, and units, which we exploit using granular administrative data and various complementary reduced-form approaches. The two-percentage-point transfer tax cut substantially raised transactions among the young, but we can rule out even modest medium-run increases in homeownership. Instead, we document large timing and bunching responses. Prices of qualifying units increased by between 1.2% and 1.8%, suggesting that the tax cut mostly benefitted sellers. Welfare simulations reveal that, while the tax cut reduced transfer tax distortions and increased overall economic surplus, gains accrued primarily to upper-middle-income households.
title: Do Transfer Tax Cuts Create Homeowners?

abstract: This study examines how armed conflict in Ethiopia (2020–2023) affected access to general and maternal health care, using Young Lives longitudinal data matched with ACLED conflict records and qualitative evidence collected in 2025. Overall, 26.2% of respondents reported conflict-related barriers to health care, while 23.6% of new mothers experienced difficulties accessing maternal services. Greater exposure to conflict events or fatalities significantly increased the likelihood of unmet general health care needs. Maternal health care was particularly affected in 2020. Qualitative findings highlight damaged facilities, staff and medicine shortages, transport disruptions, unavailable maternal services, and missed vaccinations. The findings underscore the need to protect health facilities and workers, sustain medicine supplies and referral systems, and ensure timely care during conflict.
title: The Impact of Armed Conflict on Access to Health Care in Ethiopia: Evidence from Young Lives

abstract: Large cities gain abstract jobs and shed routine jobs faster than small ones. Whether this divergence arises because workers change location or because workers’ labor market careers differ across locations matters for welfare and policy, and cross-sectional data cannot tell the two apart. Using the French administrative panel DADS–EDP, we decompose the change in each occupation’s employment share, by city size, into within-city occupational switches, cross-city relocation, combined moves, and non-employment flows. The divergence is produced inside cities. Large cities move workers from routine to abstract jobs at twice the rate of small cities, and this flow more than accounts for the urban gap in abstract employment. The routine decline is absorbed by upgrading into abstract work, not by downgrading into manual services. This urban elevator predates the 1994 onset of French polarization and operates within occupations: holding worker characteristics and the occupation of origin fixed, staying in a large city raises the rate of upgrading by about 40%, for college and non-college workers alike. The evidence places the burden of explanation on agglomeration forces rather than on the sorting of heterogeneous workers across cities.

title: Urban Elevators and the Geography of Labor Market Polarization

abstract: We revisit the sheepskin effect in a unified framework to examine the separate roles of both ethnicity and immigration in returns to academic qualifications for UK-educated minorities and white natives, defined by country of birth. Conditional on attained academic qualifications, we find that white natives generally have higher returns to years of schooling. In contrast, minorities have larger returns for higher academic credentials than whites, especially for minority immigrants. RIF-based Unconditional Quantile Effect results suggest that systematic differences by ethnicity in degree subjects, university selectivity and degree quality account for most of the differential sheepskin effects. Importantly, leveraging the 1988 GCSE reform and subsequent expansion in higher education opportunities, we further show that ethnic minorities disproportionately benefited from an increase in returns to first degrees, especially for those with lower-middle abilities. Our findings are consistent with endogenous human capital investment and differential assortative matching of skills to jobs by minorities in anticipation of labour market discrimination.
title: What Explains the Differential ‘Sheepskin Effect’ by Ethnicity and Immigrant Status in the UK? The Role of Degree Choice and Occupational Sorting

abstract: The issue of trust and cooperation in employment relations is a complex one as multiple actors are involved. The issue not only refers to the vertical relationship between workforce and management, but also to horizontal relationships among workers. Moreover, worker representation through unions or works councils often plays a role in employment relations. This brings a series of further important aspects to the issue – the quality of the relationship between a worker representation body and management, the impact of worker representation on the quality of worker-management relationships, the quality of the relationship between workers and their representation body, and the impact of worker representation on the quality of relationships among workers. This chapter provides a review of the econometric evidence on the determinants, outcomes and dynamics. Econometric research shows that trustful and cooperative employment relations not only have microeconomic consequences at the individual or firm level. They also have macroeconomic implications for the performance of labor markets.
title: Trust and Cooperation in Employment Relations: Evidence

abstract: This chapter provides an overview of the rapidly evolving economics literature on mental health, focusing on research published since 2015. This literature has grown substantially, reflecting the increased recognition of the prevalence and economic costs of mental illness, declining stigma, and the growing availability of data on mental health. In addition to the economic costs of mental illness, the review focuses on four broad classes of determinants of mental health: endowments, economic resources, education, and trauma. We also examine the determinants and effects of mental health treatment. Finally, we discuss how certain features of mental illness, including its episodic and recurrent nature, pose challenges for the canonical health capital model.
title: Economics of Mental Health

abstract: We estimate the effects of introducing paid parental leave on infant health and health care use in a setting with universal access to health care. We exploit Australia’s 2011 reform through a regression discontinuity difference-in-differences design and administrative records covering all New South Wales births. We find a 1.3 and 1.2 percentage points decline in probability of any specialist visits and any prescription medications in the first year, and no effects on hospital and emergency presentations. The reduction in any medication use persists until age five and the reduction in specialist visits is concentrated among young mothers who were least likely to have had employer leave and among clinically high-risk births. Survey data suggest that the reform eased financial strain and preserved employment, pointing to improved parental resources and time.
title: Time, Money, and Infant Health: The Consequences of Paid Parental Leave

abstract: We complement existing literature by estimating determinants of the total fertility rate for 183 economies between 2000 and 2023. Methodologically, we utilise pooled OLS and economy/country fixed-effects regressions and complement them with exploratory random forests, which take into account non-linearities and interaction effects. Variable importance measures suggest that after two indicators for life expectancy, GDP per capita, and schooling, pension coverage is among the more important predictors of fertility. Our results suggest that acknowledging the costs of childbearing and childrearing in pension systems may be a method to address declining fertility.
title: Does Pension Coverage Predict Fertility? International Evidence from OLS, Fixed Effects and Machine Learning Random Forests

abstract: The world's top destination country for migrant workers, the United States, is enacting a set of unprecedented taxes on high-skill immigration that include charging employers roughly $100,000 for each foreign worker they hire using the H-1B visa. The US government has relied on one academic study to design the tax and evaluate its impact on high-skill immigration under the H-1B quota, an impact the study estimates at zero by measuring the wage differences between H-1B and native workers. This paper precisely replicates the study's method and finds that its conclusion rests on three major flaws, each of which renders its results difficult to interpret. The study mismeasures the wage gap between H-1B and native workers, misinterprets any negative wage gap as reflecting markdowns rather than task specialization, and carries the wage results into a policy simulation whose central estimates are invariant to the wage gap: they predict an identical (null) effect on immigration for any H-1B wage gap including zero. Improved methods are required to offer regulators useful information on the effects of this large shift in immigration policy.
title: Taxing High-Skill Immigration: Fundamental Problems in Evaluating Immigrant-Native Wage Gaps and the H-1B Visa Tax

abstract: Nine in ten children in Sub-Saharan Africa cannot read a simple text by the age of ten, and most are taught in a language they do not speak at home. The dominant policy response is home language instruction. Using a unique dataset of 1,718 formerly out-of-school children in an accelerated learning programme in Ghana and Liberia, we compared matched pupils, who spoke the language of instruction at home, with mismatched pupils, who did not. First, understanding of the language of instruction is a better predictor of reading progress across countries than language match. Second, reading is shaped by classroom characteristics: the more classmates shared a mismatched pupil’s home language, the worse that pupil read. Third, language understanding can be built: most mismatched pupils developed oral proficiency in the language of instruction within a single programme cycle, the classroom’s language mix predicted whether they did, and those who did read better. No language policy can match the home language of every child, but every child should be taught to understand the language of the classroom.
title: Language Match Is Fixed, Language Understanding Can Be Built: Rethinking Home Language Instruction in Sub-Saharan Africa

abstract: Students must allocate their time during tertiary education, but the evidence on the earnings value of their achievements and experiences is dispersed across separate literatures. We systematically reviewed 38 quantitative studies examining academic performance, delayed graduation, internship experience, student employment, and student leadership in relation to earnings during the first five years after graduation. We distinguish correlational evidence from quasi-experimental estimates and interpret the findings against theoretical mechanisms linking credentials to earnings. We find that academic performance is generally positively associated with earnings and has the most consistent quasi-experimental support for earnings premiums, especially at labour market entry. Internships can also yield substantial earnings gains, but estimates vary more across programmes and research designs. Student employment is generally associated with higher earnings when field-related, but the evidence does not establish a general causal premium. Delayed graduation and student leadership remain comparatively understudied.
title: What Pays beyond the Degree? A Systematic Review of Educational Credentials and Early-Career Earnings

abstract: This paper examines how top income earners respond to changes in the personal labor income tax schedule, uncovering both own- and cross-tax base responses. We exploit a 2012 tax reform in Uruguay that generated quasi-random variation in top marginal rates within the top 1% of the labor income distribution. We use difference-in-differences and administrative records linked at the individual level. We estimate an own-tax base intensive margin elasticity of 0.82 and extensive margin semi-elasticity of 3.36. Extensive margin responses are mostly driven by taxpayers shifting from the personal labor income tax base toward corporate income or capital income tax bases (semi-elasticities of -1.00 and -0.61, respectively). Our estimates suggest that the reform was effective in increasing tax revenues, with efficiency costs representing 31% of the projected increase. However, it had limited impact on inequality, most likely due to its narrow scope and income shifting toward tax bases with lower and flat rates. Overall, our results indicate that policy efforts aiming to reduce inequality by increasing top marginal tax rates should also focus on limiting income shifting opportunities to strengthen their redistributive effects.
title: How Do Top Earners Respond to Taxation? Own- and Cross-Tax Base Responses, Efficiency, and Inequality

abstract: This paper examines worker preferences for AI-enabled changes in task composition and possibly facilitating job characteristics in a discrete choice experiment among workers in a multinational manufacturing firm. The firm implements an AI tool transforming workers’ core task of classifying electronic components in two successive stages: (1) augmenting AI including a decision support feature and (2) autonomous AI automating easy classification tasks. Workers have to choose between jobs that differ in five characteristics: the AI-enabled change in their classification task, breaks, autonomy, training, and a salary increase. The results show that workers prefer the changes induced by augmenting AI over autonomous AI. Workers would forgo a moderate salary increase when their core task is supported by the augmenting AI. Moreover, the perceived usefulness of the augmenting AI negatively moderates the preference for autonomous AI. These results suggest that human-AI complementarity is favorable while simultaneously posing disadvantages for stepwise implementation strategies.
title: AI Implementation at Work: Worker Preferences for Task Changes

abstract: Access to professional jobs, particularly in large, high-wage firms, is a key determinant of career success for university graduates. Graduates from less advantaged backgrounds are less likely to gain access to these jobs. We use unique recruitment data from 17 large employers’ graduate intake programmes to explore why. While applicants from lower socio-economic and ethnic minority groups are well represented among the applicant pool, they disproportionately do not receive job offers, even when considering similar applicants. Large gaps appear at the blind pre-interview screening stage. We demonstrate that this is unlikely to reflect screen ing on expected productivity. This raises questions of bias in screening tests and the potential for shifts to the use of more automated hiring tools to exacerbate existing labour market inequalities.
title: (Knock, Knock) Knocking on the Glass Door: Socio-economic Inequalities in Access to High-Pay Careers

abstract: How do adolescents respond to occupational advice from their parents? We study this question in a survey experiment with matched parent-adolescent data (N=1,227) from Germany. We ask parents how strongly they would recommend their own occupation and that of the other parent, randomly reveal these recommendations to their child, and then measure the child’s occupational preferences. Revealing parental advice does not generally increase adolescents’ interest in their parents’ occupations. Instead, adolescents often adjust their preferences in the opposite direction to parental recommendations. These non-conforming responses are particularly pro-nounced among older adolescents and when parents and adolescents envision different occupational fields for the adolescent’s future.
title: Rebellious Teenagers? Parental Advice and the Occupational Preferences of Their Children

abstract: Reducing working hours is widely believed to lower output. I study more than 250 legislated reductions in normal working hours worldwide over the past century. Using local projections and synthetic controls, I find that actual hours fell when reforms applied, but output did not: a decade later, GDP and GDP per capita were about 3 per cent higher than in a plausible counterfactual. Classifying each reform by its motivation and dating the start of its discussion, I find similar results for reforms whose timing was unrelated to economic conditions. Historically, on average, legislated working time reductions have not lowered output.
title: Shorter Hours, Lower Output? Evidence from a Century of Working-Time Legislation

abstract: Nearly half of 15-year-old students in OECD countries, and more in some poorer countries, use AI weekly for learning. Generative AI makes schoolwork help cheap for connected students, but cheaper help need not yield lasting learning. We link the economics of supplementary education with learning science to examine how effort, entry costs, public provision and assessment shape AI tutoring’s benefits. Randomized trials find gains and losses varying by setting, use and outcome, while lasting, equitable gains remain uncertain. We distinguish program effects from generative AI’s contribution, compare full costs with alternatives, and propose decision rules and a trial design.
title: From Cheap Answers to Lasting Learning: AI Tutoring and Educational Inequality

abstract: Hardly any study investigates the relationship between wage mobility, poverty, and inequality. Analyzing Turkish SILC data during 2006-2024, we find more wage mobility for longer time periods, particularly in the past three years. Wage mobility has largely been due to wage redistribution, rather than wage growth. Individual factors that are positively associated with higher-than-average wage mobility include working above the minimum wages, older age, having a formal job or being non-poor. Managers and professional workers or workers in large firms have most wage mobility, while workers in small to medium firms have lower-than-average to average wage mobility. Those working in the agricultural and industrial sectors have lowest wage mobility. Further regression analysis suggests that upward wage mobility and being able to maintain high wage over time are respectively associated with increases of at least 12% and 18% in poverty reduction.
